 8 Ways Social Security Will Change in 2027
 Josh Koebert 2026년 11월 20일 금 오전 10:19 UTC 0 
Social Security doesn't stand still. Every year, the Social Security Administration (SSA) adjusts a long list of dollar figures tied to the program, from the size of monthly checks to how much income gets taxed to fund them. For 2027, the agency has confirmed a fresh round of updates that touch retirees, survivors, people with disabilities, and workers still paying into the system.
Some of these changes mean bigger checks. Others mean a bigger tax bill or a higher bar to qualify for benefits in the first place. None of them are permanent, either. These figures are recalculated annually based on wage and price trends, so what applies in 2027 won't necessarily carry over to 2028 or beyond.
Here's a complete look at what's confirmed to change, who it affects, and what it could mean for your finances and retirement plan .
 Find Out: 13 moves seniors could benefit from but often forget about. 
 1. The cost-of-living adjustment is rising 3.6%
The SSA announced a 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) for 2027, a yearly increase designed to help benefits keep pace with inflation. The adjustment applies to nearly 72 million Social Security beneficiaries starting in January 2027 and to about 7.3 million Supplemental Security Income (SSI) recipients starting December 31, 2026, according to the SSA.
On average, retirement benefits will increase by about $75 per month. The COLA is calculated using the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (CPI-W), as set out in the Social Security Act.
This affects nearly every beneficiary of the program. The practical implication: Your exact new benefit amount will show up in your COLA notice, available online through your personal my Social Security account starting in late November 2026, or by mail in December for those without an online account.

 2. Average benefit amounts are increasing across the board
Beyond the headline COLA percentage, the SSA's 2027 fact sheet details how the increase plays out across different groups of beneficiaries:
The estimated average monthly benefit for all retired workers rises to $2,170 in January 2027, up from $2,095 before the COLA was applied. 
 An aged couple both receiving benefits can expect an average of $3,355. 
 A widowed mother with two children could see an average of $4,074. 
 An aged widow or widower alone could see an average of $2,005. 
 A disabled worker with a spouse and one or more children could see an average of $3,077, and the average for all disabled workers rises to $1,701.
This matters because these averages give a realistic benchmark, as opposed to the maximum benefit, which only a small share of beneficiaries ever receive. The practical implication: Compare your own benefit statement against these averages to understand where you stand, but remember these are averages, not guarantees for any individual.
 3. The maximum taxable earnings amount is climbing to $192,300
The taxable maximum, also called the contribution and benefit base, is the most income subject to Social Security payroll tax each year. For 2027, that cap increases to $192,300, up from $184,500 in 2026, according to the SSA. The payroll tax rate itself remains 6.2% for employees and employers each, or 12.4% for self-employed workers.
This affects higher earners specifically. Workers earning at or above the new cap will pay Social Security tax on an additional $7,800 of income compared with 2026. The practical implication: Someone earning the new maximum would contribute $11,922.60 to the program for the year, matched by their employer, a noticeably larger bill than in 2026.

 4. The earnings-test limits are increasing for early filers still working
People who claim Social Security before reaching full retirement age (FRA), the age at which you qualify for 100% of your calculated benefit, can have part of their benefit temporarily withheld if they earn above certain thresholds while working. 
 For 2027, the limit for people who won't reach FRA all year rises to $25,560 annually, or $2,130 per month, up from $24,480 in 2026. The SSA withholds $1 in benefits for every $2 earned above that limit.
For people who reach FRA sometime in 2027, the limit is higher: $67,920 annually, or $5,660 per month, up from $65,160 in 2026. In that case, $1 is withheld for every $3 earned above the limit, and only earnings in months before reaching FRA count. Once someone reaches FRA, there's no limit on earnings at all.
This affects early filers who continue working. The practical implication: Withheld benefits aren't lost forever. The SSA recalculates your monthly benefit upward once you reach FRA to account for the months withheld.

 5. The maximum possible benefit is rising to $5,358 at age 70
The SSA publishes example maximum benefit figures based on a worker who earned at or above the taxable maximum in every one of roughly 35 working years. For a worker retiring at full retirement age in 2027, that maximum is $4,188 per month, up from $4,152 in 2026, according to the SSA.
It's worth noting this FRA figure isn't the single highest benefit available. Workers who delay claiming until age 70 can receive a larger amount, since delayed retirement credits add roughly 8% per year of growth between FRA and age 70. For 2026, the SSA states that figure at $5,181 per month for someone retiring at 70, but it's going up to $5,358 for 2027.
This affects a small slice of beneficiaries. Only a small percentage of retirees ever hit the true maximum, since it requires both high, sustained earnings and careful claiming timing. The practical implication: For most people, the average benefit figures above are a far more realistic planning number.
 6. Work credit requirements are getting more expensive to earn
To qualify for Social Security retirement benefits, most workers need 40 credits, generally earned over 10 years of work, with a maximum of four credits available per year. The amount of earnings needed to earn one credit rises to $1,970 in 2027, up from $1,890 in 2026, according to the SSA. That means it will take $7,880 in covered earnings to earn the maximum four credits for the year, compared with $7,560 in 2026.
This affects younger or newer workers still building eligibility, as well as anyone with a sporadic work history trying to reach 40 lifetime credits. The practical implication: Earning more credits than the minimum doesn't increase your benefit amount. It's your 35 highest-earning years, not your credit count, that determines your monthly payment.

 7. Disability thresholds for substantial gainful activity are increasing
Substantial gainful activity (SGA) is the SSA's term for a level of work and earnings that generally disqualifies someone from being considered disabled for benefit purposes. For 2027, the SGA threshold for non-blind individuals rises to $1,770 per month, up from $1,690 in 2026. For blind individuals, it rises to $2,950 per month, up from $2,830, according to the SSA.
This affects applicants for Social Security Disability Insurance (SSDI) and current disability beneficiaries who are working or considering work. The practical implication: Earning above these thresholds generally signals to the SSA that a person isn't disabled under the program's rules, which can affect both initial eligibility and continuing benefits.
 8. The Trial Work Period threshold for disability beneficiaries is rising
Separately from SGA, the SSA sets a lower earnings threshold called the Trial Work Period (TWP), which lets current SSDI beneficiaries test their ability to work without immediately losing benefits. For 2027, that threshold rises to $1,270 per month, up from $1,210 in 2026, according to the SSA.
This affects people already receiving SSDI who want to attempt a return to work. The practical implication: Earning above the TWP threshold in a given month counts toward using up trial work months, a separate and distinct limit from the SGA threshold that determines initial eligibility.
 SSI payment standards and resource limits are also changing
For recipients of Supplemental Security Income (SSI), a needs-based program for people with limited income and resources, the federal payment standard rises to $1,029 per month for an individual in 2027, up from $994, and to $1,544 per month for a couple, up from $1,491, according to the SSA. The SSI student earned-income exclusion also rises, to $2,500 per month and $10,080 per year.
Notably, the SSI resource limits are not changing. They remain $2,000 for an individual and $3,000 for a couple, figures that have stayed flat for years under current law.
This affects SSI recipients, including many disabled or low-income older adults. The practical implication: While payment standards rise with wage trends, the frozen resource limits mean SSI recipients still face tight restrictions on savings and assets, something to be aware of when weighing eligibility.
 Living on Social Security? 20 little-known things that could help with bills. 
 Bottom line
These 2027 changes show how interconnected Social Security's moving parts really are. A single COLA announcement from the SSA triggers ripple effects across benefit checks, tax bills, disability thresholds, and eligibility rules alike. None of these dollar figures are set in stone; they're recalculated annually based on wage growth and inflation, so expect another round of updates for 2028.
For a closer look at how these changes could affect an individual situation, the SSA's online benefit estimator and a my Social Security account remain reliable tools for checking personalized figures. And if money is tight, consider ways to free up your retirement budget .
